Your brain cells use a gene that can still jump around your DNA.
Half of your genome is made of old jumping genes, called transposons.
Almost all of them froze millions of years ago. They can't move anymore.
But a gene called BC200 is different. It works in your neurons, and it can still move.
Cornell researchers spotted it in an odd place: inside a human poxvirus.
That virus infects skin cells, so the team thinks BC200 jumped from skin into the virus.
Normally, once a jumping gene gets a real job, it stops jumping. This one never did.
BC200 exists only in humans and close primate relatives, and it also shows up in sperm and egg cells.
The next question: is it jumping inside cancer cells, where it's abnormally active?
